1	# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code
2	
3	**seeding**
4	: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
5	
6	**base build**
7	: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.
8	
9	**old code**
10	: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.
11	
12	Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.
13	
14	## Finding or building a base build
15	
16	- If your brief names a base build, use it.
17	- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
18	  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
19	  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
20	  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
21	- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.
22	
23	      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
24	      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
25	      ant compileAll
26	      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
27	      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
28	      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean
29	
30	If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.
31	
32	## Seeding a worktree
33	
34	A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.
35	
36	Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.
37	
38	    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
39	
40	- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
41	- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
42	- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
43	- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
44	- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
45	- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
46	- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
47	- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.
48	
49	## Running the old code
50	
51	If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.
52	
53	`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:
54	
55	    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
56	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
57	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
58	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
59	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM
60	
61	- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
62	- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
63	- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
64	- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).
65	
66	To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:
67	
68	    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
69	        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss
70	
71	The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".
72

1	# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild
2	
3	**tree**
4	: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.
5	
6	**library order**
7	: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.
8	
9	**DSL grammar**
10	: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.
11	
12	**parser directory**
13	: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.
14	
15	## Setting up each call
16	
17	Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:
18	
19	    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
20	    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
21	    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
22	    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
23	
24	- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
25	- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
26	- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.
27	
28	The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:
29	
30	- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
31	- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).
32	
33	If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.
34	
35	The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.
36	
37	With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:
38	
39	- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
40	- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.
41	
42	## Two layers of code
43	
44	The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.
45	
46	The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the run time. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.
47	
48	The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:
49	
50	- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
51	- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
52	- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
53	- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.
54	
55	An edit makes stale what was built from it:
56	
57	- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
58	- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
59	- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
60	- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.
61	
62	## The caches
63	
64	All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:
65	
66	- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
67	- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
68	- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
69	- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).
70	
71	Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).
72	
73	## The library order
74	
75	The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.
76	
77	Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:
78	
79	- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
80	- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.
81	
82	Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:
83	
84	    cd ProjectFortress
85	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
86	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
87	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
88	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
89	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s
90	
91	Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.
92	
93	- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
94	- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
95	- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.
96	
97	## Name resolution
98	
99	- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
100	- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
101	- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
102	- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
103	- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.
104	
105	## Building
106	
107	Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.
108	
109	- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
110	- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
111	- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
112	- `ant cleanCache` deletes the caches, whatever their stamp.
113	- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
114	- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
115	- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.
116	
117	## After an edit of the library
118	
119	The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.
120	
121	- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
122	- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
123	- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
124	- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.
125	
126	## Symptoms of a skipped step
127	
128	If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:
129	
130	- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
131	- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.
132	
133	If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.
134	
135	Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:
136	
137	- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
138	- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.
139	
140	Two more facts help you read a run:
141	
142	- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
143	- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.
144

1	# Running tests
2	
3	**track**
4	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.
5	
6	**shard**
7	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.
8	
9	**code state**
10	: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.
11	
12	## The two suites
13	
14	`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:
15	
16	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
17	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
18	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
19	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.
20	
21	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.
22	
23	`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
24	
25	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
26	
27	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
28	
29	The two suites work in the same way:
30	
31	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
32	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
33	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
34	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
35	
36	To run a suite:
37	
38	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
39	- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
40	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
41	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
42	
43	## The switches that the harness reads
44	
45	Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.
46	
47	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
48	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
49	- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
50	- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
51	- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
52	- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.
53	
54	## Outside the gate
55	
56	- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
57	- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
58	  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run, a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`interpreter.md`, "Natives") or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.
59	  - Print the driver with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md#Commands worked out'`. Save the first script that it prints, under "The demo driver", without the text around it, as `tmp/run-demos.sh` in your tree.
60	  - From the tree's root, after you set up the call, run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. It runs long, so run it in the background with a log (`session.md`, "Long commands"). It runs the demos under walk one at a time and writes `tmp/demos/summary.tsv`.
61	  - The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line, must read 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. A demo reaches its end if it exits 0 and its output holds no "fail" in upper or lower case.
62	  - If your change breaks a demo and you know how to repair the demo, repair it in the commit of your change. Otherwise, report the demo, its output and the ledger row that holds the missing feature, as a defect that your change makes or uncovers.
63	- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).
64	
65	## When to run a whole suite
66	
67	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
68	- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk, of a phase that both paths share or of such a class under `nativeHelpers/`, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
69	  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
70	  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
71	  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`), the parser or such a class, run both.
72	- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
73	- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
74	- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the run time (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
75	- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.
76	
77	The suites do not check these:
78	
79	- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
80	- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
81	- the linker's aliasing of apis;
82	- `fortress unparse`;
83	- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
84	- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.
85	
86	If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.
87	
88	## One test, or a few
89	
90	Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.
91	
92	### Interpreter tests
93	
94	Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:
95	
96	    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
97	        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]
98	
99	- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
100	- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
101	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
102	- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
103	- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
104	- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
105	- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.
106	
107	To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:
108	
109	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss
110	
111	The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").
112	
113	### Compiled tests
114	
115	Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).
116	
117	The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.
118	
119	    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
120	        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1
121	
122	- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
123	- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
124	- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
125	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
126	- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
127	- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.
128	
129	To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:
130	
131	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test
132	
133	Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.
134	
135	## One unit-test class, or one track
136	
137	To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.
138	
139	To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:
140	
141	- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
142	- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
143	- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
144	- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.

1	# The Claude Code session: the Bash tool, long commands, waits and stops
2	
3	**prompt cache**
4	: API's copy of a conversation's context. It lives five minutes for an agent and one hour for the main session. Each request to the API within that time reads the cache and renews it. The first request after a longer wait writes the whole context again: late in a long task, hundreds of thousands of tokens.
5	
6	**interrupt**
7	: Stop of the session's turn, by the stop button. It kills every agent that runs in the background at that moment, of the Agent tool or of a Workflow.
8	
9	**stop of the process**
10	: End of the session's Claude Code process. It kills every agent. It keeps the conversation, the transcripts and the disk: worktrees, uncommitted edits and logs. A command started with `nohup` (below) survives a stop, but not a restart of the machine.
11	
12	**automatic permission check**
13	: Check that approves each tool call in auto mode. It can refuse a call, also a call that the curator approved in chat.
14	
15	## The Bash tool and waits
16	
17	The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).
18	
19	- In an agent, keep every wait under 270 s.
20	- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.
21	
22	## Long commands
23	
24	If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it detached with `nohup`, after the setup lines, whose exports it inherits. Write the command and the log in the line itself:
25	
26	    nohup bash -c '( ant compileAll ) > tmp/build.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/build.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
27	
28	Keep the setup lines and the `nohup` line as separate lines. `A && nohup B &` runs `A` in the background too, so its `cd` and its exports do not reach the lines after it in the same call.
29	
30	The log gets the output, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`. The automatic permission check refuses a shell function that passes the command to `bash -c` in a variable, because it cannot read the command.
31	
32	The shell function `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 270 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0: ant's `BUILD` and `Total time:`, JUnit's `OK (`, `FAILURES!!!` and `Tests run:`, and `EXIT=`. If not, it returns 1.
33	
34	Run `wait_for` until it returns 0, each time in a new Bash call. Give that call a `timeout` above 270 s, such as 300000 ms. Define the function in each call that uses it. Grep the log for the lines that you need.
35	
36	    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 270]; call again until it returns 0
37	        local n=0 max=${2:-270}
38	        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=270 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 270 ] && max=270
39	        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
40	            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
41	            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
42	        done
43	        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^OK (\|^FAILURES!!!\|^Tests run:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
44	    }
45	
46	If your brief says that you run beside a batch, a run of other agents that build and test at the same time, run every build, suite, stage and program under `nice -n 19`, after `nohup`. Run one command of your own at a time that starts a JVM. The JVMs that it starts count with it.
47	
48	- Start such a command only when the `available` column of `free -g` shows 6 GB or more. If it shows less, check again in each call of a wait, as `wait_for` waits, for at most 30 minutes. If it still shows less, start nothing and report back.
49	- A timed run of the checker is a plain run, under the rules for every other run here; it takes no lock and waits for no other work.
50	
51	## Stopping processes
52	
53	Stop only the processes that run under your tree's path. To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.
54	
55	Kill by process id, with `kill <pid>`. A pattern, as in `pkill -f`, also matches other agents' copies of the same scripts, and your own call's shell, which it then kills.
56	
57	## After an interrupt or a stop of the process
58	
59	If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop of the process:
60	
61	1. Read what is on disk first: `git log` and `git status` in your tree, and your logs.
62	2. If a step's log has ended and the tree has not changed since, the step is done. A log has ended if it has its `EXIT=` line, or its verdict or table is complete.
63	3. If a log has no `EXIT=` line yet, its command may still run. Look for its process under your tree's path. If it runs, wait for it with `wait_for`.
64	4. Continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed.
65	
66	## When the automatic permission check refuses a call
67	
68	- Do not try for the same result with another tool, by another route or in a later turn.
69	- Report the refusal and what was not done because of it. The way through is the curator's: manual approval for the session, or an allow rule for the command (`/permissions`).
70

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
14	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
15	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
16	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
17	
18	## How to commit
19	
20	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
21	
22	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
23	
24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
27	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
28	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
29	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
30	
31	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
32	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
33	
34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it.
35	
36	## Pushing
37	
38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
39	
40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
42	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
43	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
44	  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:
45	
46	         git push origin main
47	         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
48	         git push origin main:blinded-fable
49	
50	     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
51	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
52	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.
53

1	# The library
2	
3	The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
4	
5	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
6	- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
7	- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
8	- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.
9	
10	## How loops and reductions call the library
11	
12	The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:
13	
14	- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
15	- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
16	- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.
17	
18	These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.
19	
20	## The curator's decisions on the library
21	
22	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
23	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
24	- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
25	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
26	- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
27	- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.
28	
29	## Designing a change
30	
31	- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
32	- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
33	- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
34	- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
35	- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
36	- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
37	- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
38	- In an api, declare each top-level function and each member of a trait or object at the header that the component gives it. A function's header is its name, its static parameters with their bounds, its modifiers, its `throws` clause, its parameters' modifiers and types, and its return type. A function's parameters' names and a `where` clause do not count, but each static parameter's name counts (ledger row 836). Give an object's value parameters the api's names, because they are its fields (`compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path"). In the cases below, change the component's header to the api's, not the api's to the component's. The examples are in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`.
39	  - The member's body already answers the api's type. `RR64`'s `opr |\self/|`, `opr |/self\|` and `truncate` answer `ZZ64`, because they call `Float`'s natives, which answer `ZZ64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:184-191`).
40	  - The api cannot name the component's type. `Array2`'s and `Array3`'s `bounds` and `zeroIndices` answered types of `RangeInternals`, which depends on this api. They now answer the api's `CompactFullRange` types, which those types extend.
41	  - The api's type is wider, and the overrides and bodies use only that type. `DelegatedIndexed`'s `generator` answers the api's `Generator[\E\]`, as `FlatString`'s override does.
42	
43	  In the api, write `abstract` on each member that the component leaves without a body.
44	- The compiled checker's export check matches each api member with a component member of the same name and header. It matches these members in these ways:
45	  - A field, as `x: ZZ32` in an api's trait: by a component field of its name, its type and its modifiers other than `var`. A component's getter does not match it, so declare a field in the component too (ledger row 842).
46	  - An object's value parameter: by its type and its modifiers other than `var`, but not by its name.
47	  - A getter written `abstract`, as `abstract getter one(): T`: by a component getter at its header, or by a component field of its name and type that is neither `hidden` nor `private`. A `hidden` field has no getter.
48	  - Another member written `abstract`: by a component member at the api's header, with a body or without one.
49	
50	  Each entry of the check's error names a trait or object and only its first member that differs. After you fix that member, check again to see the next. These steps run the check:
51	  - For a component of a compiled program or test: `fortress compile`.
52	  - For the one library's `FortressLibrary` component: the count stage (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time").
53	  - For the other thirteen components that the gate's distance stage checks: that stage. When a rung needs it, the brief gives its command.
54	  - For another component of the one library: no step, until the switch-over.
55	- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
56	- Write a new native as a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, and bind it with `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")`. Both paths run it. Give it the Java types that carry the declared types (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"). Write a glue class under `interpreter/glue/prim/`, which only walk runs, only where no Java type carries a declared type, as for `IntLiteral`'s bindings. Most of the library's bindings still name glue classes. A native is an edit of Java: rebuild (`build-and-caches.md`, "Two layers of code"), and test it on both paths (`compiler.md`, "Natives").
57	- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.
58	
59	## Editing
60	
61	A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.
62

1	# Exploring: a question that the record does not settle
2	
3	The record keeps what earlier workers found, and they met many of the same questions. Workers have called a thing absent or new when the record already held it.
4	
5	## The choices that are yours
6	
7	The curator settles every conflict and every question about a decision of the curator. Any other choice is yours only if it meets all four of these conditions:
8	
9	- It changes only one area.
10	- It changes no line of the model program.
11	- It changes no decision of the curator.
12	- It can be undone.
13	
14	## Weighing the sources
15	
16	The type group is the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, from 2009 to 2012. Where their late positions disagree with the specification's earlier text, the late positions weigh more. These positions are:
17	
18	- the exclusion rule;
19	- compiled code specialised to each instantiation of a generic, which they kept;
20	- the compiled number tower, which they flattened in 2009 and 2010;
21	- the 2012 write-up on the Return Type Rule (`Papers/Types/journal/`);
22	- the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`).
23	
24	The team's later work is outside the original tree. It is in these places:
25	
26	- `research/extracts/`: the POPL 2019 paper, Steele's talks of 2015 and 2016, and the project's web sites with the post of July 2012 that ended the project;
27	- the reading of the team's 2012 patents: `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md`.
28	
29	If a conflict or a decision not taken needs the designers' reason for a rule, print the row of its design area. WORD is a word of the area, such as `coercion`, `juxtaposition`, `dispatch` or `Arrays`. A word can match several rows, each about 1 to 2 KB.
30	
31	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#The map, by design area@WORD'
32	
33	Then open the sources that the row names. Among them are the `\note{}` boxes and the team's written rationale in the Internal Document appendix: `Specification/appendices/FAQ.tex` and `future.tex`. The row also names the later works that speak to its area, after the words "after the repository (§7)". To read what one of them covers and does not cover, print its row of the map's section "After the repository". WORD is a word of its title, such as `Polymorphic`, `patents`, `JuliaCon` or `Wrapping`. A row is about 1 to 2 KB.
34	
35	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#After the repository@WORD'
36	
37	When your report describes the team's sources on a question, say which of them is one of the late positions above. If the question is about a type rule, also name each later work that you checked.
38	
39	## The procedure
40	
41	1. Search the record with the queries in `records.md`. If two of the team's sources disagree, look for the construct in `revival-changes.md` before you search the record.
42	2. If the record or `revival-changes.md` settles the question, go back to building. Cite what settles it.
43	3. If you have evidence against a decision of the curator, read its POSITIONS entry and the notes that it names. If the decision used your evidence, go back to building.
44	4. Search the original tree. These help: the feature table and the phase map (`compiler.md`, "Before an edit"), the `\note{}` boxes and the map of design areas ("Weighing the sources" above), and the history of a file (`records.md`, "The repository's history").
45	5. Before you write that something does not exist, search the record for it, INDEX included (`index:WORDS`).
46	6. Decide whose choice it is, by "The choices that are yours" above.
47	7. Record each defect that you found as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says. If you make the choice and repair the defect, that is its item 1. If the question stays open, it is its item 3. Record a finding that is not a defect, such as a fact about the original tree, as `records.md`, "Writing to the record", says.
48	8. If your brief does not let you edit the ledger, put the ledger row in your report:
49	   1. Write the row in a file, in the form that `records.md` gives for a new row.
50	   2. Run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py check --rows FILE`. It counts the `?` in the number cell as a broken rule. Correct the row until the check names no other rule.
51	   3. Copy the row into your report.
52	9. If the question touches a passage of the specification, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
53	10. If the choice is yours, make it. Report it as a decision.
54	11. If the choice is the curator's, report it as a decision not taken. Give these:
55	    - the question;
56	    - each source, and its date ("Weighing the sources" above says what else to note);
57	    - each possible solution, and what it changes;
58	    - which solution keeps the current behaviour.
59	12. If you cannot get some evidence in your task, say in your report what is missing and how to get it.
60
